To address this issue, Parameter-Efficient Fine-Tuning (PEFT) methods have been introduced, enabling adaptation with a reduced number of trainable parameters. Among these techniques, Low-Rank Adaptation (LoRA) has gained widespread recognition for its efficiency and ease of integration. This survey provides a thorough exploration of LoRA, covering its mathematical principles, implementation techniques, and real-world applications. By comparing LoRA to traditional full fine-tuning and other PEFT methods, we highlight its ability to maintain strong performance while significantly cutting down on computational overhead. Empirical evaluations across various NLP benchmarks further demonstrate its effectiveness in reducing memory consumption without sacrificing accuracy. Beyond its advantages, we also examine the challenges associated with LoRA, such as rank selection sensitivity, compatibility with different model architectures, and potential hardware optimizations. Additionally, we discuss promising future directions, including hybrid fine-tuning strategies, dynamic rank adjustment, and expansion into multi-modal learning. By enabling more efficient adaptation of complex models, LoRA represents a crucial advancement in scalable fine-tuning. This survey aims to serve as a valuable resource for researchers and practitioners looking to leverage LoRA for optimized model training across diverse applications.<\/jats:p>","DOI":"10.36227\/techrxiv.174015835.57150536\/v1","type":"posted-content","is-referenced-by-count":1,"title":["Revolutionizing Large Model Fine-Tuning: The Role of LoRA in challenge for Whisper's decoder that relies on static languageprefix tokens, which results in cross-attention misalignment, autoregressive insertion loops and hallucination where the transition in languages occurs. This paper presents a comparative study of two adaptation strategies, viz textual prompt injection and Low-Rank Adaptation (LoRA), for improving Whisper's robustness on Hindi-English codeswitched speech recognition. By using the OpenSLR-104 code-switched corpus alongside Common Voice (Hindi) and LibriSpeech (English) for cross-lingual and forgetting analysis, the study shows that while prompt injection reduced Global WER from 1.91 to 1.63 by providing decoder context, it fails to restructure the frozen cross-attention weights and remains prone to repetition loops. LoRA adaptation also improves monolingual Hindi recognition (WER: 0.82 \u2192 0.6), with only a limited degradation on monolingual English (WER: 0.03 \u2192 0.06), thereby indicating limited catastrophic forgetting. A CTC baseline (Wav2Vec2 XLS-R 300M) is also evaluated and shown to fail (100% WER) when processed on code-switched audio, thus highlighting the importance of the capacity of autoregressive language models on mixed-script speech. (LLMs) has generated substantial interest in techniques for grounding model responses in domain-specific knowledge. This paper presents a systematic empirical comparison of five LLM augmentation strategies applied to document-grounded question answering over a corpus of academic research documents: (1) Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) with FAISS vector search and bibliography filtering, (2) Knowledge Graph (KG) augmentation using NetworkX-based co-occurrence graphs, (3) a Multi-Step Reasoning Agent employing iterative plan-searchreason-synthesise cycles, (4) parameter-efficient fine-tuning of TinyLlama-1.1B via Low-Rank Adaptation (LoRA), and (5) a Hybrid approach combining all three retrieval strategies to feed the fine-tuned model. Using TinyLlama\/TinyLlama-1.1B-Chat-v1.0 as the base model across all conditions, we evaluate each approach on five domain-relevant research questions using keyword-overlap relevance scoring and response-time measurement. The Multi-Step Agent achieved the highest average relevance score (0.88), followed by the Hybrid approach (0.67) and Fine-tuning (0.46), while vanilla RAG performed the worst on direct relevance despite lower latency.
